summary: Help 10–11 year-olds EXPLAIN (not just list) how lifestyle choices affect how body systems function, using cause-and-effect reasoning grounded in the circulatory, digestive and muscular systems they already know. The teaching core is linking a specific choice (exercise, diet balance, harmful substances) to a bodily effect — for example exercise strengthens the heart and muscles and also benefits mental health — distinguishing immediate effects (heart rate rises now) from long-term effects (heart strengthens, resting pulse lowers, weight changes), and backing the reasoning with real measurement (pulse before/after exercise). Treat drugs, alcohol and tobacco factually and age-appropriately, and avoid moralising 'good vs bad' lists or stigma around weight.
misconceptions: Treating the topic as 'good vs bad' foods/behaviours rather than understanding the mechanism of impact on body function.
Thinking exercise only builds muscles, missing its effect on the heart, lungs and healthy weight.
Believing effects are only immediate (or only long-term), rather than both (heart rate now, strengthening over time).
Assuming 'healthy' means thin or that weight alone measures health, rather than how well systems function.
Thinking small amounts of harmful substances have no effect on how the body works.

activities.title: Lifestyle simulator: run a body over time by changing choices
steps: Set a character's choices using controls: an exercise/activity level, a diet-balance control, and toggles for harmful substances (tobacco, alcohol, misused or illegal drugs). Medicines are also drugs and, used correctly, can help the body.
Push the exercise level up and observe the live heart-rate meter climb immediately.
Let a few simulated weeks pass and watch the 'heart & muscle strength' and 'healthy weight' meters change over time.
Then lower activity and set the diet to very sugary/fatty, and watch the weight and heart-strain meters move the other way.
Add tobacco and observe a lung-function meter fall.
Run the SAME starting body twice with different choice settings and compare how differently it ends up functioning.
In words, state one immediate effect and one long-term effect of a choice you set, naming which body system it affected.
activities.insight: A lifestyle choice is a cause that changes how a specific body system functions, with both immediate and longer-term effects. In the model, the same starting body can end up functioning very differently because of the choices made; in real life, genes, age and other factors also play a part.

activities.title: Pulse before and after exercise (real measurement)
steps: Measure and record your resting pulse (beats per minute).
PREDICT what your pulse will do after exercise and why.
Do one minute of vigorous activity such as star jumps.
Measure your pulse again immediately afterwards.
Time how long it takes to return to your resting rate.
Compare results across people and discuss why a fitter person's pulse tends to recover faster and why their resting rate is often lower.
Connect what you measured to the simulator: find the same rise reflected in the on-screen heart-rate meter.
activities.insight: The heart's response to exercise is real, measurable and personal: heart rate rises during activity and recovers afterwards, and greater fitness is linked to a lower resting rate and faster recovery.

activities.title: Explore-a-body: reveal how each choice affects a system, with myth-busters
steps: Select the heart to reveal what regular exercise does to it (strengthens it, lowers resting heart rate).
Select the lungs to reveal how smoking affects them.
Select muscles and the digestive links to reveal how diet balance supplies energy and nutrients.
Reveal that regular exercise also benefits mental health, not only the heart and muscles.
Open myth-buster prompts such as 'Does exercise only build visible muscles?' and read the correction.
For each revealed link, say aloud which choice is the cause and which system is affected, and whether the effect is immediate, long-term, or both.
activities.insight: Each lifestyle choice maps to specific effects on specific body systems — exercise is more than bigger limb muscles (it strengthens the heart, lowers resting pulse and supports mental health), and harmful substances impair organ function.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, categorise and explain WHY
steps: Match each lifestyle choice to its effect on a specific body system.
Categorise choices by whether they help or harm how a system functions.
Answer explanation questions that require the MECHANISM (e.g. why does regular exercise lower resting heart rate?), not just a 'good/bad' label.
For at least one item, write a sentence naming the choice, the system affected, and whether the effect is immediate or long-term.
activities.insight: Explaining a lifestyle impact means stating the mechanism linking a choice to a body system's function, distinguishing immediate from long-term effects.

activities.title: Ask the expert: questions for a GP or sports coach
steps: Think of your own questions, such as 'What happens to my heart if I train regularly?' or 'Why is smoking bad for my lungs?'
Ask an in-role GP or coach persona and listen to factual, age-appropriate answers.
Follow up to find out whether an effect is immediate or long-term, and which system it touches.
Summarise one answer in your own words, naming the choice, the system and the effect.
activities.insight: Lifestyle-impact reasoning can be driven by a learner's own curiosity, including sensitive topics like drugs, handled factually.

checkQuestion: Someone says 'exercise just makes your arm and leg muscles bigger — it doesn't really change anything inside your body.' Is that true? What does regular exercise do to your heart, and why would that matter even when you're sitting still later?
checkAnswer: It's not true. The heart is a muscle, and regular exercise makes it stronger so it pumps more blood per beat; this lowers the resting heart rate and delivers oxygen more efficiently, even at rest. Exercise also benefits the lungs, helps maintain a healthy weight, and improves mental health — it's far more than bigger limb muscles.
